query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The resistance of high‐entropy alloys (HEAs) to simultaneous wear and corrosion arises from their ability to form a stable, self-healing passivating surface film enriched in noble elements that is intimately supported by a refined, high-entropy microstructure. This film minimizes local chemical gradients while the uniform, nanocrystalline grain structure inhibits crack initiation and propagation during mechanical stress.
generation.material_initial_state: A nanocrystalline refractory high‐entropy alloy with a multi‐principal element, predominantly single-phase solid solution (or a controlled dual‐phase microstructure) that exhibits uniform elemental distribution.
generation.intervention: Expose the HEA to an environment combining mechanical sliding (wear) and a corrosive medium (e.g., a chloride or acidic electrolyte, or molten salt) under controlled temperature and load conditions.
generation.conditions: Simultaneous mechanical load (to induce wear) and corrosive attack with moderate to harsh chemical aggressiveness under temperature regimes that allow both passive film formation and mechanical deformation (e.g., room to moderately elevated temperatures).
generation.structural_mediator: The fine nanocrystalline grain structure and any beneficial dual-phase interfaces (if present) that promote preferential enrichment of noble elements at the surface, leading to a continuous, adherent oxide/passivation layer.
generation.mechanism: Under combined mechanical and corrosive stresses, the high configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion kinetics promote uniform elemental distribution and nanostructuring that facilitate the formation of a protective, self-healing passivation film. This film minimizes localized anodic sites and resists removal during mechanical wear, thereby decreasing both chemical dissolution and abrasive material loss.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline alloy (such as a conventional or coarse-grained alloy lacking these features), the HEA will exhibit a lower wear volume and reduced corrosion rate. The synergistic protection should be most evident under conditions where the chemical attack is sufficiently moderate to allow passivation, but not so severe that mechanical wear completely removes the film.
generation.baseline: A matched conventional alloy or a HEA variant with a coarser microstructure and less favorable elemental segregation, tested under identical wear and corrosion conditions.
generation.boundary: The prediction is expected to hold under moderate-to-severe corrosive and wear conditions where the protective film can form and persist. It may fail in ultra-high wear conditions, extremely aggressive corrosive media, or temperatures that disrupt the film formation (or alter the grain structure significantly).
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative scale of the improvement and the precise critical thresholds for the transition between protective passivation and film failure remain uncertain and likely depend on the specific alloy composition and processing history.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: the high-entropy alloy with a refined, nanocrystalline structure and a baseline alloy with coarser grains (or an intentionally perturbed composition designed to diminish preferential passivation). Subject both sets to a combined wear-corrosion test using a tribometer integrated with an electrochemical cell (using a representative corrosive medium such as a chloride solution) at controlled temperature. Measure wear rates (volume loss), friction coefficients, and corrosion rates (e.g., via potentiodynamic polarization).
measurements: Wear volume loss via profilometry or microscopy
Corrosion current density and polarization resistance from electrochemical measurements
Surface chemical composition and film integrity via XPS or Auger spectroscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in both wear and corrosion resistance (i.e., similar or higher degradation metrics) compared to the baseline sample under identical test conditions, the hypothesis that the synergistic formation of a self-healing, protective passivation film, mediated by a refined high-entropy microstructure, governs resistance, would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. The CrMoNbWV HEA has comparable mechanical and corrosive properties with the WNbMoTaV type HEA, but at the same time has a reduced density: CrMoNbWV—10.55 g/cm

Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe.
